title: A Proud King Brought Low
overview: Babylon's most powerful king tells, in his own words, how a warning dream, a sudden loss of his sanity and its return taught him that God rules over every kingdom, including his.

parts.label: The king's public letter (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: The chapter is written as Nebuchadnezzar's own announcement to his whole empire. Before telling an embarrassing story about himself, he praises the God of Israel, whom he calls the Most High, as a king whose rule never ends.

parts.label: The dream of the tree (vv. 4-18)
parts.note: At the height of his peace and success, the king dreams of a giant tree that feeds and shelters every creature, until a holy messenger from heaven orders it cut down to a stump bound with iron and bronze. A huge tree was a familiar picture of a powerful empire, and the metal band probably means the stump is kept safe to grow again, though some read it as the king being restrained.

parts.label: Daniel delivers hard news (vv. 19-27)
parts.note: Daniel is shaken, because the tree is the king himself, who will lose his mind and live outdoors like an animal for seven 'times,' probably seven years, until he admits that God gives power to whoever God chooses. The surviving stump means his throne will come back, and Daniel urges him to turn from wrongdoing by doing right and showing mercy to the oppressed.

parts.label: Pride and the fall (vv. 28-33)
parts.note: A year later, walking in his royal palace, the king boasts that he built great Babylon by his own power, and at once he loses his reason and lives in the fields like an animal. Babylonian inscriptions do show him boasting about his buildings but record no madness, and many scholars think this story echoes a similar tradition about a later king, Nabonidus.

parts.label: Sanity and praise return (vv. 34-37)
parts.note: When the king looks up toward heaven, his mind comes back, and he praises God as the true ruler whose decisions no one can overrule. He gets his throne back, and his last line sums up the story: God is able to humble the proud.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this chapter records an actual episode in Nebuchadnezzar's life or is a story told to make a point about pride and power, a question tied to the lack of outside evidence and the similar tradition about Nabonidus.
think: How much of what you have achieved feels like your own doing, and how much came from things outside your control?
